source: Hitchcock, Stanford Encyclopedia: Critical Thinking (definitions)
finding: Definitions compete. Dewey (1910) says careful consideration of a belief in light of its grounds. Ennis counts 14 scholarly and 3 dictionary definitions and treats them as rival conceptions. Facione's 1990 expert statement lists evidential, conceptual, methodological, criteriological and contextual considerations.
numbers: Ennis: 14 scholarly + 3 dictionary definitions; Ennis lists 12 aspects (1962).
quote: active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge in the light of the grounds that support it
limits: No single agreed definition. Entry is a synthesis, not data.
agent_relevance: Pick an operational definition (grounds-checking of claims) rather than a trait label.

source: Hitchcock, SEP: skills versus dispositions
finding: Abilities and dispositions are listed separately. Dispositions include open-mindedness, wanting evidence, willingness to suspend judgment, persisting in complex tasks, abandoning unproductive strategies. Abilities include observing, questioning, inferring, argument analysis, judging.
numbers: 9 initiating dispositions and 9 ability families listed.
limits: Lists are conceptual, not empirically derived factors.
agent_relevance: Dispositions map to guardrails (stop rules, seek disconfirming evidence). Abilities map to operators.

source: Hitchcock, SEP: generalism versus subject specificity
finding: McPeck (1981) denies general thinking skills exist, since thinking is always about some subject. Critics note general writing and speaking skills. Entry separates conceptual, epistemological and empirical forms of the specificity claim. Evidence that instruction transfers across domains is called scanty.
numbers: no numbers
limits: Philosophical dispute; empirical forms partly open.
agent_relevance: Supports carrying domain content in context instead of a domain-free reasoning module.

source: Hitchcock, SEP: summary of Abrami et al. (2015)
finding: Dialogue, anchored instruction and mentoring each raised effectiveness; combining them was best. Separate CT instruction plus subject teaching beat either alone but not significantly.
numbers: Direction only; no effect sizes on this page.
limits: Secondhand summary; primary paper not opened (403).
agent_relevance: Intervention hint: combine explicit method, real problems and feedback.

source: Hitchcock, SEP: Siegel's ideal and bias critiques
finding: Siegel (1988) gives four reasons for CT as an educational ideal: respect for persons, self-sufficiency, initiation into rational traditions, democratic citizenship. Paul's strong-sense CT adds dialectical engagement with opposing views to counter egocentric bias. Critics say CT overweights reason over emotion and care.
numbers: 4 Siegel reasons; no test data.
limits: Normative argument, not tested.
agent_relevance: Paul's strong sense is a model for an adversarial self-review step.

source: Hitchcock, SEP: test coverage differences
finding: Standard tests measure different constructs. Cornell Level X has 24 of 76 items on credibility. Cornell Level Z has 4 of 52 on experimental design. CCTST has 11 of 34 on inference and 5 of 34 on argument analysis. Facione (1990c) and Kuhn (1991) found no sex difference.
numbers: Item counts as stated.
limits: Scores from different tests are not interchangeable.
agent_relevance: Any LLM CT benchmark inherits its test's narrow coverage.

source: Willingham (2007) Critical thinking: why is it so hard to teach?
finding: CT programs mainly improve performance on problems like those practiced. Success depends on domain knowledge and on metacognitive strategies. Knowing to look for deep structure helps but needs knowledge to apply.
numbers: Band-problem experiment: 19% used the analogous garden solution unaided, 35% with a hint. Treasure-cave puzzle: about 75% of US students solved it versus 25% of Chinese students; reversed for a Chinese folk tale puzzle.
limits: Popular review, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Hints help only partly. The agent needs retrieved domain knowledge, not only a CT prompt.

source: Willingham (2007): weaknesses of CT program evaluations
finding: Evaluations of thinking-skills programs share four flaws: one post-test only, no control group, no active comparison, no transfer test. Few were peer reviewed. Philosophy for Children: of 8 studies, 3 had design problems; of the 5 left, 1 of 3 reading studies and 2 of 3 reasoning studies found gains.
numbers: 8 studies; 5 usable; reading 1/3 significant; reasoning 2/3 significant.
limits: Secondhand counts from two reviewers. Older programs (Tactics for Thinking sold 70,000 guides).
agent_relevance: Gains from scaffolds also need controls and transfer tests.

source: Willingham (2007): A Nation at Risk claim
finding: The 1983 report claimed nearly 40 percent of 17-year-olds could not draw inferences from written material and only one-fifth could write a persuasive essay. Two decades of programs brought little visible improvement.
numbers: about 40% and about 20%
limits: Policy claim, quoted secondhand.
agent_relevance: Background on why the ideal is contested.

source: Huber & Kuncel (2016) Does college teach critical thinking? A meta-analysis (AERA snapshot)
finding: College is linked to real gains in CT. Four years of college moves a typical student from the 50th to the 72nd percentile.
numbers: 71 research reports; 48-year span; 50th to 72nd percentile (about d 0.59, my conversion).
limits: Only the summary page was read. Not an experiment: maturation and selection are not separated.
agent_relevance: Human ceiling for trained CT is moderate, so large scaffold-gain claims need strong controls.

source: Huber & Kuncel (2016), moderators from a search summary
finding: From a search summary only: curriculum-wide CT efforts did not reliably beat normal college gains; nursing students did not gain more; gains looked smaller in later decades.
numbers: not verified
limits: Search snippet, not read. Unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Check before using.

source: Arum & Roksa (2011) Academically Adrift (via Wikipedia summary)
finding: About 45 percent of students showed no significant gain in critical thinking, complex reasoning and writing in the first two years of college (CLA).
numbers: Over 2,300 undergraduates at 24 institutions; 45% no gain at 2 years.
limits: Page lists critics but gives no replication numbers. A 4-year figure was not on the page.
agent_relevance: The CLA is a performance task, like how LLM answers are judged.

source: Abrami et al. (2008, 2015) meta-analyses of CT instruction
finding: From memory, not opened (403). Roughly 117 studies and average g about 0.34 in 2008; 341 effect sizes and g about 0.30 in 2015. Mixed instruction and dialogue, authentic problems, mentoring raised effects.
numbers: 2008 g+ about 0.34; 2015 g+ about 0.30. Recalled, verify.
limits: Page returned 403. SEP (b04) agrees on direction only.
agent_relevance: Moderate effect size is the realistic target.

source: Facione (1990) Delphi Report, APA
finding: From memory: about 46 experts reached consensus that CT is purposeful, self-regulatory judgment. The ERIC PDF is a scanned image; no text extracted.
numbers: about 46 panelists (recalled).
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Core skills map to scaffold steps.

source: Human Ennis-Weir norms (Hollis et al., as reported in the o1 study)
finding: Human EWCTET scores rise with education. 100 online participants averaged 14.31 (SD 8.45). Postgraduates 18.39 (SD 6.59), undergraduates 11.51 (SD 8.23), p below .001.
numbers: N=100; maximum score 29.
limits: Online convenience sample, no CT intervention. Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Human norm for LLM comparison.

source: Hatcher and Davidson & Dunham: Ennis-Weir training effects (as summarised in the o1 study)
finding: A year-long CT course at Baker University raised Ennis-Weir means from 5.8-9.4 to 11.8-13.8 (gains 2.8 to 6.0 points). In a Japanese EFL college, trained group scored 6.6 and control 0.6 (p below .001).
numbers: Treatment n=17, control n=19; Baker over four years.
limits: Small N. Secondhand summary.
agent_relevance: Instruction gains are real on the trained test, which fits Willingham's caution.

source: o1-preview on the Ennis-Weir essay test (arXiv 2412.05753)
finding: o1-preview scored 20 of 29 zero-shot, 26 with a college-student role prompt and 27 with a graduate role prompt. The paper reports mean 24.33, above undergraduates (13.8) and postgraduates (18.39).
numbers: 3 prompts, one scored run each; z = 1.60 and 0.90 against the two human groups.
limits: Mean is of three prompt variants, not independent trials. Authors scored with the rubric. The 13.8 comes from a training study. Role prompt moved score by 6 to 7 points.
agent_relevance: Prompt wording moves the score as much as the human education gap. Report variance.

source: Huang et al. (2024) LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without oracle labels, self-correction lowers accuracy. GPT-3.5 on CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8 to 38.1 after one round and 41.8 after two. GPT-4 on GSM8K fell from 95.5 to 91.5 then 89.0.
limits: Generic prompts. With oracle labels gains were large (GPT-3.5 HotpotQA 26.0 to 49.0), so gains came from knowing when to stop. Earlier positive claims used oracles.
agent_relevance: Reflective critique with no outside check can hurt. Critique steps need an external signal.

source: Huang et al. (2024): why self-correction fails
finding: GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7 percent of the time on GSM8K. When it changed, it more often went from right to wrong than wrong to right. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo kept answers more often.
numbers: 74.7% retained on GSM8K for GPT-3.5.
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2-70b-chat only.
agent_relevance: The model cannot judge its own reasoning. Add a verifier or tools.

source: Lu et al. (2023) Critique Ability of Large Language Models (CriticBench)
finding: Critique is hard for most models and appears only at large sizes. Self-critique is especially hard. Models critique worst where they are most uncertain. A self-check baseline helps.
numbers: About 3K queries over math, code and QA.
limits: Abstract only; model names and scores not read.
agent_relevance: Skeptical review works only on large enough models; flag weak spots.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The impact of generative AI on critical thinking (CHI)
finding: Survey of knowledge workers using Bloom's taxonomy as the definition of CT. Higher confidence in GenAI goes with less CT. Higher self-confidence goes with more. Effort shifts to verification, integration and stewardship.
numbers: 319 workers; 936 examples; CT enacted in 555 (59.29%); less effort reported in 72% Knowledge, 79% Comprehension, 69% Application, 72% Analysis, 76% Synthesis, 55% Evaluation.
limits: Self-reported and correlational. Bloom framing is one choice among competing definitions (b01).
agent_relevance: Confidence in the tool lowers checking. Keep guardrails that force checks regardless of how sure the model sounds.

source: Lee et al. (2025): task-confidence coefficients
finding: Confidence in AI doing the task predicts less perceived effort for five of six Bloom activities (all except Application). Effects are small.
numbers: Knowledge beta -0.11 (p=.029); Comprehension -0.13 (p=.014); Analysis -0.15 (p=.003).
limits: Self-report, ordinal regression.
agent_relevance: Small effects: do not overclaim.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT
finding: In essay writing, LLM users showed the weakest EEG connectivity, lowest ownership, and trouble quoting their own essays. Switching LLM users to brain-only reduced alpha and beta connectivity.
numbers: 54 participants in sessions 1-3, 18 in session 4; groups LLM, search, brain-only; four months.
limits: Abstract page only was read. Small N, preprint, EEG interpretation debated. Not a CT test.
agent_relevance: Offloading is measurable; relevant to human-agent design.

source: Not Too Short, Not Too Long (2026): LLM answer length and error detection on Watson-Glaser items
finding: People judged GPT-5 answers to 15 modified Watson-Glaser items. Accuracy at spotting wrong answers was 0.245 for short, 0.542 for medium and 0.307 for long outputs.
numbers: 24 participants, 15 items (8 correct, 7 wrong outputs); correct-output accuracy 0.715 short, 0.811 medium, 0.795 long; wide CIs.
limits: One model, n=24, no p-values or odds ratios reported, length confounded with reading time.
agent_relevance: Even with explanations people miss most errors: show checkable evidence, not longer text.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (PNAS)
finding: From memory, not opened (403): about 1,000 high-school maths students; unrestricted GPT access raised practice scores by about 48 percent but lowered later exam scores by about 17 percent; a tutor version with guardrails removed the harm.
numbers: about 1,000 students; +48% practice; -17% exam (recalled, verify).
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Supports guardrails over free assistance.
